newsitem.title: ITALY: Finmeccanica, GEC in defence venture.
newsitem.headline: Finmeccanica, GEC in defence venture.

text.p: Italy's Finmeccanica and Britain's General Electric Co Plc said on Thursday they would set up a wide ranging joint venture to create a major force in Europe's splintered defence industry.

The preliminary deal, which has been under discussion since last March and should be finalised before the end of the year, involves the two firms taking minority stakes in some of their respective defence operations.

"This satisfies the strategic demand for a European alliance which will create the critical mass necessary to remain competitive with large groups operating at a world level," state-controlled Finmeccanica said in a statement.
It added that other European defence manufacturers might eventually join the Anglo-Italian partnership.
At the heart of the accord is an equally-owned joint venture which will work on missile systems, naval systems, ground-based radar, command and control systems and air traffic control.

GEC's defence arm, GEC-Marconi, will acquire between a 30-49 percent stake in Alenia Difensa's avionics division, a Finmeccanica unit, while Alenia will take a similar stake in GEC-Marconi's armaments and armoured vehicle business.
"This joint venture is in effect a merger of these businesses," Dr Alan Kemp, the director of corporate strategy at GEC-Marconi, told Reuters in London.
"It is a very significant development and reflects a lot of work on both sides," he added.
The combined turnover of the businesses involved was put at around two billion sterling and represented the majority of the the two European group's defence operations, Finmeccanica said.

The deal was a major coup for Finmeccanica, Italy's second largest industrial company after car maker Fiat, which has struggled in recent years, plunging 540.4 billion lire ($318 million) into the red in 1996.

The group, controlled by state holding Iri, has been seeking strategic alliances across its range of aerospace, defence, transport and energy activities in a bid to prepare itself for planned privatisation.

For GEC, the joint venture marks the first big deal struck by new managing director George Simpson. Earlier this week Simpson announced a major shake-up for GEC, putting its defence unit GEC-Marconi the new heart of the group.
Finmeccanica and GEC have already established links through a range of previous defence projects and Kemp said the geographic fit between the two firms was good.

"We are strong in different markets to the Italians. They are strong in the Middle East, Latin America and the British are strong in the Far East, the old Commonwealth countries, Canada and North America, for example," he said.
He added that the emphasis would be less focused on cost savings and more on widening the product range and sharing research and development costs.
"It's a consolidation of the industry rather than rationalisation of capacity," he said.
Europe's defence industry, still struggling to come to terms with the end of the Cold War, has been left in the shade by recent huge mergers in the U.S. defence sector.
Finmeccanica said the GEC joint venture would be a smaller force than the U.S. giants.

"Nonetheless the formula of the deal is designed...to attract other partners to accelerate the process of consolidation in the European defence industry which up until now has been slowed by political fragmentation and persistent nationalism," its statement said.
